one_line: Walkthrough of MySQL's four log types (error, general, slow query, binary) on Ubuntu, then shipping them and server metrics to Better Stack with a slow-query anomaly alert.
summary: The presenter explains the four MySQL log types and where each lives on a Linux server: the error log (startup, shutdown and runtime diagnostics), the general query log (connects, disconnects and every query, off by default), the slow query log (queries over a configurable time), and the binary log (data-changing events used for replication and restore). Each is enabled or tuned either at runtime with SET GLOBAL or persistently in my.cnf under [mysqld], followed by a service restart. The slow log is verified with SLEEP(1) versus SLEEP(3) against a 2-second threshold, and mysqldumpslow is used to summarize it. The second half sets up Better Stack: a MySQL log source, a read-only metrics user, the Better Stack MySQL exporter, and Vector to forward logs. It then shows Live Tail, a MySQL dashboard template, and an automatic anomaly alert on slow queries per second. The content is generic MySQL operations with a vendor product walkthrough for the centralization half; nothing is AI-specific.

key_ideas.idea: The error log is the first place to look when MySQL won't start or is misbehaving, but it always contains startup and shutdown messages, so entries alone do not indicate a fault.
key_ideas.detail: Default path on Ubuntu is /var/log/mysql/error.log. Each line carries timestamp, thread id, label, error code, subsystem and message. The verbosity is set with log_error_verbosity: 1 logs errors only, 2 (default) errors and warnings, 3 adds informational messages. The presenter recommends keeping the default.

key_ideas.idea: The general query log records every connect, disconnect and received SQL statement, which makes it the best tool for seeing exactly what a client sent. It is off by default.
key_ideas.detail: It is a debugging log rather than a performance log. The speaker notes it does not map one-to-one to commands the user typed: session init statements and server-restart commands also appear.

key_ideas.idea: The slow query log captures only queries that exceed a configurable threshold, which makes it the practical way to find queries worth optimizing.
key_ideas.detail: Threshold is long_query_time in seconds (demo uses 2; the speaker suggests raising it if normal queries already take around 2 seconds). Log rows show query time, rows sent and rows examined.

key_ideas.idea: The binary log stores data-modifying events (for example CREATE, DELETE even with no matched rows) and not reads; it serves replication and point-in-time recovery, and it is not meant to be read by hand.
key_ideas.detail: Use SHOW BINARY LOGS and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin' to list files and locate them. Files are in /var/lib/mysql, with an index file.

key_ideas.idea: Local log files are hard to monitor at scale, so the presenter ships them to a hosted log service and gets metrics from the same server.
key_ideas.detail: Setup uses a Better Stack source with its token, a dedicated read-only metrics user instead of root, the Better Stack MySQL exporter script, and a Vector install script that wires up the logs. Live Tail then shows entries as they arrive.

key_ideas.idea: A built-in MySQL dashboard template with anomaly-based alerting on slow queries per second catches regressions without hand-written thresholds.
key_ideas.detail: The alert compares the current rate against a moving average and can notify by email, SMS or Slack. The presenter says percentage-change and fixed-threshold rules are also available.

techniques.name: Enable general log at runtime
techniques.how: Run `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'general%';`, then `SET GLOBAL general_log = 'ON';` and `SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/general.log';`. The file must be writable by the mysql user.
techniques.when: Temporary debugging of what a client actually sent, without a restart.

techniques.name: Enable logs persistently in my.cnf
techniques.how: Edit /etc/mysql/my.cnf (sudo nano). Under [mysqld] add: general_log = 1, general_log_file = /var/log/mysql/general.log, slow_query_log = 1, slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql/slow.log, long_query_time = 2. Then `sudo systemctl restart mysql.service`.
techniques.when: Logs that must survive restarts; the config-file method is the one the presenter prefers for clarity.

techniques.name: Slow query log threshold check
techniques.how: Run `SELECT SLEEP(1);` (not logged) and `SELECT SLEEP(3);` (logged at long_query_time = 2). Then inspect the file with `sudo mysqldumpslow /var/log/mysql/slow.log`.
techniques.when: Confirming the threshold works and summarizing slow queries in readable form.

techniques.name: Locate binary logs
techniques.how: Inside the mysql client: `SHOW BINARY LOGS;` and `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';` (the log_bin_index and base name show the path, /var/lib/mysql). Do not parse them by hand.
techniques.when: Before recovery or replica setup, to know which files to keep.

techniques.name: Ship MySQL logs and metrics to Better Stack
techniques.how: In Better Stack, go to Logs > Sources > Connect source, choose platform MySQL, and copy the source token. Follow the docs' logs-and-metrics option: create a dedicated monitoring user (named BetterStackMetrics in the video) with a password of your own, run the provided exporter install script, then run the Vector install command with the token substituted (chosen OS: Ubuntu). Verify in Live Tail.
techniques.when: Central log search and dashboards without SSH-ing into each server.

techniques.name: Dashboard template plus anomaly alert
techniques.how: In Better Stack: Dashboards > Create dashboard > search the MySQL template > Add. The template comes with an automatic alert on slow queries per second. Adjust the rule to a percentage change or a fixed threshold, and route it to email, SMS or Slack.
techniques.when: Detecting a sudden rise in slow queries without writing your own detector.

tools: Better Stack (logs, Live Tail, dashboards, alerts)

numbers.claim: log_error_verbosity default is 2 (errors and warnings); 1 = errors only, 3 = adds informational messages.
Demo slow-query threshold: long_query_time = 2 seconds; SLEEP(1) is not logged, SLEEP(3) is. The speaker suggests a higher threshold, around 4, if normal queries already take about 2 seconds.
Demo buffer pool size is 128 MB, and the server had been up for 49 seconds at the time of the dashboard screenshot.
Better Stack's free tier is mentioned as the starting point (no pricing given).

hot_takes: Quality capped at 3, not 4: the centralization half is a walkthrough of one vendor's product, with a free-account pitch, but the local-log half is accurate, practical and reproducible.
Not AI-related; relevant to our observability layer, not to agent-specific design.
The general query log is presented as a debugging tool and the speaker does not discuss its overhead or retention, which matters on busy production servers.
Anomaly-based alerting on slow queries per second is presented as an automatic default, with no discussion of false positives or tuning.

relevance.why: L4 observability and L3 storage: the slow-query threshold plus anomaly alert pattern applies to Postgres or ClickHouse latency monitoring, though the video covers MySQL only.
relevance.action: When wiring slow-query monitoring for the Postgres/pgvector or ClickHouse tiers, copy the pattern: a threshold log (long_query_time-style), a summary tool, and an anomaly alert on slow-query rate, then check it with a deliberately slow query.

relevance.why: Database logging is unrelated to the Claude Code harness.
